reason: The text emphasizes strict hierarchy at multiple levels as fundamentally important to its narrative structure. The divine hierarchy is central: God maintains supreme authority over the divine council (בְנֵי הָאֱלֹהִים) and Satan, who must obtain permission and report to God. Social hierarchy is explicitly valued: Job is described as the greatest of all 'the children of the east' (מִכָּל־בְּנֵי־קֶדֶם), underscoring his superior status. Family hierarchy is evident in references to 'the firstborn brother's house' (בְּבֵית אֲחִיהֶם הַבְּכוֹר) and Job's authoritative role as patriarch who sanctifies his children and makes offerings for them. The entire opening establishes Job's prominence and moral preeminence ('תָּם וְיָשָׁר' - blameless and upright) as essential to the narrative. Rather than discouraging hierarchy, the text treats hierarchical relationships—divine, social, and familial—as structurally necessary and morally significant.
